To express possibility: il est possible que, il se peut que + subjunctive.
To express probability and certainty: il est probable que, il est certain que, je suis sûr que + indicative.
To express doubt: je doute que, je ne suis pas sûr que, il n’est pas certain que + subjunctive.
To use the adverbs: peut-être, sans doute, probablement, certainement.
To avoid the trap: "sans doute" means "probably", not "without doubt".
Monday, 15 April, eight in the morning. On the La Duchère site, Radu and the Tête d’Or park gardener, Monsieur Fournier, are planting the lime tree before the ceremony.
There. The hole is deep enough. We can put it in the ground. Gently… it’s young, it’s fragile.
Do you think it’ll take root? It’s spent ten years in a pot.
It’s very likely it’ll take root. Lime trees are hardy. But it’ll need watering often during its first summer.
The children will look after it. Yanis has already asked me if he can be in charge of watering. And when will it flower?
I doubt it’ll flower this year. It may produce a few flowers in June, but it’s more likely to wait until next year.
Pity. I’d have liked Hélène to see it in bloom.
It’s almost certain she’ll come. The doctor said yes last night. But she may only stay a few minutes. She’s still weak.
(looks at the sky) And it might rain. I don’t like the look of these clouds.
Don’t say that! I’m not sure we have enough umbrellas for thirty-six children.
(laughs) Don’t worry. It’ll probably pass. April clouds change their minds faster than gardeners.
Monsieur Fournier, have you seen the initials on the old lime tree? The two H’s?
I’ve been seeing them for thirty years. I always wondered who had carved them. I’d probably never have found out without you.
And now their story continues here. With this little tree.
Without any doubt. Come on, help me firm down the soil. And bring the watering can. The little one is thirsty.

French expresses how sure you are of something and changes the MOOD of the verb according to the degree. The basic rule: possibility and doubt → SUBJUNCTIVE; probability and certainty → INDICATIVE:
je doute que, je ne suis pas sûr que
il est possible que, il se peut que
il est certain que, je suis sûr que
The trap: "il est possible" takes the subjunctive, but "il est probable" takes the indicative. The logic: what is merely possible remains unreal; what is probable is almost a fact.
She may only stay a few minutes.
It may produce a few flowers in June.
"Il se peut que" is a little more spoken than "il est possible que", but it means the same.
It’s very likely it’ll take root.
I’m sure the children will look after it.

In the NEGATIVE or in a question, certainty becomes doubt → subjunctive: "Je suis sûr qu’il VIENDRA" but "Je ne suis pas sûr qu’il VIENNE". Likewise: "Il n’est pas certain que nous AYONS assez de parapluies."
"Douter que" (to doubt that) takes the SUBJUNCTIVE. Watch out for the opposite meaning of "se douter que" (to suspect), which takes the INDICATIVE:
Je doute qu’il fleurisse cette année.

False friend: "sans doute" does NOT mean "without doubt", but "probably". For "without doubt" you say "sans AUCUN doute". Also: at the start of a sentence, "peut-être" and "sans doute" require inversion or "que": "Peut-être viendra-t-elle" / "Peut-être qu’elle viendra."

On Monday 15 April, at eight in the morning, a green City of Lyon van pulled up outside the La Duchère site. Monsieur Fournier got out, with his grey beard and his rubber boots. In the back, wrapped in a blanket like a child, was the young lime tree.

Radu had been waiting for him for half an hour. He had hardly slept. He had checked the weather forecast ten times during the night: it might rain late in the morning. He had got umbrellas, tarpaulins and even a plan B, which Chloé had drawn up in triplicate.

They planted the tree together, in front of where the entrance would be, next to the spot where the bench would go. Monsieur Fournier worked slowly, with precise movements, like a surgeon. He showed Radu how to firm the soil around the roots, how to make a little hollow to hold the water.

Once the work was done, they stepped back a few paces to look at the result. The lime tree was small, barely taller than Radu, with slender branches and its first leaves of a very tender green. It looked fragile in the middle of the site, between the digger and the piles of bricks. But it was standing.

"It’ll probably outlive both of us," said Monsieur Fournier, wiping his hands. "Lime trees can live five hundred years. In a century, children will play under its branches without knowing why it’s there." Radu smiled. "There’ll be a box under the foundation stone. It’ll explain."

Around ten, the guests began to arrive. The parents from La Duchère, in their Sunday best, even though it was a Monday. The builders from the site, who had set out rows of plastic chairs. Claire Vasseur, Nathalie, Ioana with Rose-Hélène. Then the children from the orchestra, with their instruments, and Julien trying to keep them still.

The mayor arrived at half past ten, with two councillors and a photographer. He shook everyone’s hand, then went over to Radu, who was holding a small metal box. "Is that the time capsule?" he asked. Radu nodded, too nervous to speak.

But one person was still missing. Everyone was looking down the street. At twenty to eleven, Radu began to wonder whether she might not come. Perhaps the fever had gone up again. Perhaps the doctor had changed her mind. He looked at Julien. Julien looked at his phone. No message.

At a quarter to eleven, a white van appeared at the end of the street. It was the care home minibus, moving very slowly, as if it were carrying a treasure. It stopped in front of the site. The door opened. Dr Martin got out first, then Odile.

Then, with the help of a little ramp, Hélène’s wheelchair appeared. She was wrapped in a big blue coat, with a blanket over her knees and, on her head, her wedding hat. She was very pale and very thin. But she was smiling, and her eyes were shining like those of a girl arriving at a ball.

The children shouted her name. They ran towards her, then stopped a metre away, shy, as if they were afraid of breaking her. Hélène opened her arms. Inès went up first and kissed her on the cheek. Then Yanis. Then all the others, one by one, very gently, under Dr Martin’s watchful eye.

Odile pushed the wheelchair over to the young lime tree. Hélène looked at it for a long time without saying anything. She reached out and touched a leaf, very delicately, between two fingers. "It’s small," she murmured. "Its grandfather was small too, in 1962. I may not see it grow. But others will."

Then she asked where the bench would be. Radu showed her the spot, right next to the tree, marked by two stakes. Hélène signalled to Odile to push her a little closer. She looked at the two stakes, then at the lime tree, then at the grey sky. "This bench has to be comfortable," she said. "People must be able to sit on it for a long time."

At eleven o’clock sharp, the ceremony began. The mayor gave a very short speech, as he had promised. Claire Vasseur thanked the children, the parents, the region. Then the mayor invited Radu to present the project. Radu stepped forward with his notes, looked at the crowd, and forgot everything.

He looked for Ioana. She gave him a little sign: "First of all". Radu took a breath. "First of all," he began, "I’d like to tell you about a tree." And instead of talking about foundations, windows and safety standards, he told the story of the lime tree in the Tête d’Or, the two H’s in the bark, and the gardener who kept seeds.

Nobody moved. The parents were listening, the children were listening, even the photographer had lowered his camera. Monsieur Fournier, at the back, blew his nose loudly. When Radu finished, there was a long silence. Then the mayor began to applaud, and everyone followed.

Then Radu opened the time capsule in front of everyone and read out the list of what it contained. The copy of the waltz. The thirty-six drawings. The leaf from the old lime tree. The little plastic bucket, which made the children laugh. And a sealed envelope, in fine, shaky handwriting: "For those who will open this box."

Nobody knew what was in that letter. Hélène had written it during her nights of fever, in secret, and had refused to show it to anyone, even Odile. "It may be the most beautiful letter of my life," she had told Julien. "Or the silliest. Only those who read it will know."

Radu closed the box. The builders had prepared a hole in the foundations, next to the future front door, and a large cut stone, engraved with: "Musique en partage — 15 April 2029". The mayor took the trowel, spread a little cement, then turned to Hélène.

"Madame Morel," he said, "I think it’s for you to lay this box." Hélène’s eyes widened. She hadn’t known. It was Radu’s idea, which he had kept secret until the last moment, for fear she would refuse. She looked at Odile, then at Julien. Julien nodded.

Odile pushed the wheelchair to the edge of the hole. Radu put the box on Hélène’s lap. She held it against her for a moment, eyes closed. Then, with the help of Radu and Yanis, she leaned forward and placed it at the bottom of the hole, very slowly, the way you lay a baby in its cradle.

The builders laid the stone on top. The mayor spread the cement. Then he handed the trowel to Hélène, who gave the stone a little symbolic tap, like a signature. The children applauded. The photographer took a picture. And at that very moment, the clouds parted and the sun came out.

Julien raised his arms. The orchestra began to play, in the middle of the site, among the bricks and the digger. It wasn’t Henri’s waltz this time. It was a piece Julien had written for the occasion, very short and very simple, in which every instrument had its own phrase, even the buckets. He had called it "The Foundation Stone".

While the children were playing, Rose-Hélène wriggled out of her mother’s arms. She had been walking for six weeks now, still unsteadily, arms out in front. She crossed the whole site, under Ioana’s panicked gaze, towards the young lime tree. When she reached the tree, she stopped and looked up.

Then she did something nobody expected. She sat down on the ground, exactly on the spot marked by the two stakes, where the bench would be, and watched the orchestra, clapping her hands. Hélène saw her. She put her hand to her mouth. She laughed, and at the same time tears ran down her cheeks.

"Look, Odile," she murmured. "She’s already found her place." Odile squeezed her hand. Dr Martin, who was keeping an eye on her watch, checked the time: twenty minutes left. She said nothing. She just pulled the blanket a little higher over Hélène’s knees, and listened to the music too.

When the piece ended, Yanis put down his cello and went to fetch a little red watering can he had brought from home. He filled it at the site tap, then came back, very serious, and watered the lime tree slowly, the way Monsieur Fournier had shown him. "I’ll probably water this tree all my life," he announced. Nobody dared laugh.

After the concert, there was a small buffet under a marquee. Madame Mansouri had made cornes de gazelle. Sophie had brought croissants. Monsieur Mansouri had brought his oud, and Mihaela her țambal. Hélène didn’t eat anything, but she tasted a corne de gazelle to please Madame Mansouri, and said it was the best pastry of her life.

After exactly one hour, Dr Martin signalled to Odile. It was time to go back. Hélène didn’t protest. She looked exhausted, but with a happy tiredness, as after a long dance. She asked for just one thing: to go past the lime tree one last time before leaving.

Odile pushed her up to the tree. Hélène reached out one last time and touched the bark, still smooth and thin. She said nothing. Then she turned to Radu, who was standing beside her, and took his hand. "Thank you," she said simply. "Now I’ve seen everything."

Radu didn’t know what to say. He leaned down and kissed her on the forehead, as his grandmother had done with Rose-Hélène at the coach station a year earlier. Hélène smiled. Then she closed her eyes, and the minibus carried her slowly back to Fourvière.

In the evening, Julien went up to see her, as usual. She was already asleep. On her bedside table, next to the 1962 photo, Henri’s letter and the little sprig of orange blossom, there was a new photo: the one the mayor’s photographer had taken, which Radu had had printed that very afternoon.

It showed an old lady in a hat, in a wheelchair, her hand resting on a stone. Around her, children with violins and buckets. Behind her, a little tree with very green leaves. And in one corner of the photo, sitting on the ground, a one-year-old girl clapping, in a ray of sunshine.

Julien stood looking at that photo for a long time. Then he switched off the lamp and left without a sound. In the corridor he bumped into Madame Lambert, who asked him how the ceremony had gone. Julien thought for a moment. "It’s certain," he said, "that nobody will ever forget it."
